opus-5.5.text:
Thanks so much for having me, it's really great to be here.

For me, it came from the fact that I've always had two sides to my interests. Growing up I loved languages. I was fascinated by how they're structured, how different languages express the same ideas in totally different ways, and how kids pick up all of that complexity seemingly effortlessly. At the same time, I really enjoyed math and programming, the precision of it and the feeling of building something that actually works.

When I got to college and started taking computer science classes, I was looking for a way to bring those two things together. Natural language processing turned out to be the perfect intersection. It's a field where you get to think about deep questions about language, like what it means to understand a sentence and what structure is really there, but you get to approach those questions computationally, with models and data and experiments.

What made it especially exciting was the timing. It was a moment when language models were starting to get remarkably good, and that raised all these fascinating questions. These systems are learning something from text, but what exactly? Are they learning the kinds of structures linguists have described for decades, or something quite different? That tension between linguistics and engineering really drew me in, and it still motivates a lot of my research today. I like working on problems where understanding language better and building better systems go hand in hand.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks so much for having me. I think what drew me to NLP is that language is this incredibly rich, messy, human thing, and it sits right at the intersection of so many fields I care about. I've always loved linguistics, the structure of language, why grammars look the way they do, what's universal across languages and what isn't. And then computer science gives you this toolkit to actually test ideas about language at scale, with real data, rather than just theorizing.

There's also something very satisfying about working on a problem where the artifact you're studying is something everyone uses every single day. When a model gets language wrong, people notice immediately, because we all have strong intuitions about what sounds right. That makes it a really honest field in some ways. You can't hide behind abstractions.

And I came into it at a moment when things were changing fast. Large language models were starting to do things that would have seemed impossible a few years earlier, and yet there were still these very basic open questions. Why do these models learn human languages so well? Would they learn an impossible language just as easily? How much of what they pick up is about language specifically versus just statistical pattern matching? Those questions felt like they connected back to the deep linguistics questions I started with, but now with tools that could actually give you empirical answers. That combination was too appealing to pass up.

Language is something we use every day, seemingly effortlessly, but there’s so much complexity behind it. How do we convey meaning, interpret ambiguity, or understand something that isn’t explicitly stated? Thinking about those questions computationally really appealed to me. It felt like a way to work on interesting technical problems while also exploring something fundamentally human.
